title: My computer is slow
summary: Works out whether the bottleneck is startup, disk, memory, background software or simply a machine that is too old.

when.question: When is your computer slow?
when.help: Slow at startup, slow everywhere, and slow only under load have completely different causes.

options.label: Slow to start up and sign in
Slow all the time, including when idle
Slow only when opening apps or heavy work
It was fast and then became slow

startup_items.question: Does it eventually become usable, or does it stay slow afterwards too?
startup_items.help: If it recovers after a few minutes, startup software is the cause. If it stays slow, something worse is happening.

options.label: It becomes usable after a couple of minutes
It stays slow even once I am signed in

disk_health_check.question: Does Task Manager show high disk usage, often near 100%, when it is slow?
disk_health_check.help: A drive running at 100% with low CPU means the disk is the bottleneck, which usually means a failing drive rather than a software problem.

options.label: I have not checked Task Manager

cpu_or_memory.question: In Task Manager, is CPU or Memory the higher percentage?
cpu_or_memory.help: Look at the Processes tab and sort by CPU or Memory to see which program is responsible.

cpu_top_consumer.question: Is the top CPU consumer a program you recognise, or a process name you have never heard of?
cpu_top_consumer.help: Sort Task Manager by CPU. Names ending in .exe are programs. Names with no .exe, such as System, are Windows components.

options.label: It is a program I installed
It is a Windows process like System or Antimalware Service Executable
I have no idea what it is

memory_pressure.question: How much RAM does the computer have, and is memory above 85% while you are using it?
memory_pressure.help: A 4 GB machine running Windows 11 is underpowered no matter what you uninstall. More RAM needs a hardware upgrade, not a software fix.

options.label: 8 GB or more, and memory is above 85%
8 GB or more, and memory is fine

result_startup_tune.title: Trim what starts with Windows
result_startup_tune.diagnosis: Software that launches at startup is the most common cause of slow sign-in that recovers after a few minutes.
steps: Open Task Manager with Ctrl plus Shift plus Esc, then go to the Startup apps tab
Disable anything you do not recognise or use daily, especially chat clients, game launchers, cloud sync and printer utilities
Do not disable antivirus, your chipset driver, storage driver, or anything from Windows Update
Check Settings > Apps > Startup for additional entries, which covers some apps Task Manager does not show
Restart and time the sign-in to confirm improvement
If you want a clean baseline, use our system report script to see exactly what is starting
warnings: Disabling a driver rather than an app can stop hardware working. Only disable entries that are clearly applications.
Avoid 'PC optimiser' and registry cleaner tools. They commonly slow machines down further and can break Windows.

result_disk_bottleneck.title: Your disk is the bottleneck
result_disk_bottleneck.diagnosis: Disk at 100% with low CPU means the drive cannot keep up. A mechanical hard drive is the usual reason.
steps: Open Task Manager > Performance > Disk and check whether the drive is HDD or SSD
If it is an HDD, replacing it with an SSD is the single biggest speed improvement you can make, often 5 to 10 times faster
Run our disk health script to get a SMART summary and a chkdsk scan
Check free space: keep at least 15 to 20 percent free on the drive, since a full drive slows down badly
In Task Manager, identify which process is using the disk and see whether it is a known program
Check the drive's health, because a failing drive both slows down and risks your files
warnings: Back up your files before cloning or replacing a drive. Cloning to a failing drive can fail partway and leave you with neither.
Do not run chkdsk with /f repeatedly on a failing drive, since repair writes can destroy the remaining readable data. Check SMART first.

result_hdd_to_ssd.title: Replace the drive with an SSD
result_hdd_to_ssd.diagnosis: If the machine has a mechanical hard drive, no amount of software tuning will make it fast. An SSD is the right fix.
steps: Confirm your current drive type in Task Manager > Performance > Disk, or by opening This PC and checking the model number
If it is an HDD, buy an SSD of the same form factor: 2.5 inch SATA for most laptops and desktops, M.2 NVMe if the board has an M.2 slot
Clone the old drive to the new one using your vendor's cloning tool, or a free tool such as Clonezilla or Macrium Reflect
Check the new drive's health and drive letters in Disk Management after the first boot
If the drive is an HDD and you want the biggest speed gain, also add an M.2 NVMe SSD and move your games and documents onto it
Enable TRIM, which Windows does automatically for SSDs, and confirm it is on in the drive's properties
warnings: Cloning replaces the destination completely. Double-check the source and destination drives before starting, since choosing the wrong one erases data.
If your BIOS is in Legacy or CSM mode, an NVMe drive may not be visible. Switch the BIOS to UEFI mode, which requires a clean reinstall of Windows.

result_background_software.title: Reduce what runs in the background
result_background_software.diagnosis: Heavy background programs use CPU constantly even when you are not looking at them.
steps: Open Task Manager > Processes and sort by CPU to find the heaviest programs
Uninstall anything you do not use from Settings > Apps > Installed apps
Disable the ones you want to keep in Task Manager > Startup apps
Turn off background app permissions in Settings > Apps > Installed apps > each app > Advanced options
Pause OneDrive syncing in its own settings if you do not need continuous synchronisation
Update the software, since some bugs cause runaway CPU use in older versions
warnings: Do not end 'Antimalware Service Executable' or 'Service Host' processes in Task Manager. They are Windows components and ending them can cause instability.
Some security software will reinstall itself and re-enable itself if you only disable its startup entry.

result_windows_update.title: Let Windows Update finish, and check its health
result_windows_update.diagnosis: Windows components using heavy CPU in the background are usually updating, indexing or searching.
steps: Open Settings > Windows Update and let any pending updates install, ideally while the PC is plugged in
Avoid using the PC during a major update, since restarting mid-update can cause problems
Check whether Search indexing is running: Settings > Privacy & security > Windows Search > Indexing options
Limit indexing to your user folder and Program Files, and leave Windows, System32 and the whole drive root unindexed
If the same Windows process is heavy every day with no updates pending, run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth then sfc /scannow
Use our system report script to capture what is running so you can compare over time
warnings: Do not stop an update mid-way. If you must, use the pause option rather than shutting down the PC.
Turning indexing off entirely makes search slower, so restrict it rather than disabling it.

result_malware_scan.title: Check for malware
result_malware_scan.diagnosis: Unrecognised processes using heavy CPU are worth checking for malware, especially if the machine has been slow since browsing unfamiliar sites.
steps: Open Windows Security from the Start menu and run a Full scan
Run a second opinion scan with Microsoft Defender Offline, which boots into a separate environment
Check Task Manager for processes in unusual locations, since malware often runs from AppData or Temp
Install Malwarebytes for a second opinion, run a full scan, then uninstall it
Update Windows and your browser, since most malware arrives through unpatched software
Change important passwords from a different, trusted device if you suspect a real infection
warnings: Never install antivirus from a pop-up or a website you reached by clicking an ad. Use Windows Security or a vendor's official site.
Avoid 'free PC optimisation' bundles advertised by pop-ups. They are a common malware delivery method.

result_memory_apps.title: Close what is using memory
result_memory_apps.diagnosis: Above 85% memory use means Windows is constantly writing to the page file on disk, which makes everything feel slow.
steps: In Task Manager > Processes, sort by Memory to see the heaviest users
Close browser tabs you are not using, since each tab can hold a large amount of memory
Close applications that are running in the system tray but not being used
Ensure the page file is set to system-managed: System > Advanced system settings > Performance > Settings > Advanced > Virtual memory
If you use many browser tabs, install a memory-saving extension or use a browser with a tab suspend feature
Consider adding RAM if you regularly run many applications at once
warnings: Do not disable the page file entirely. Windows needs it, and setting it to zero can cause blue screens.

result_upgrade_ram.title: Add RAM
result_upgrade_ram.diagnosis: Windows 11 officially supports 4 GB, but in practice 4 GB makes a modern PC feel slow no matter what you tune.
steps: Check how much RAM you have in Settings > System > About > Installed RAM
Check the maximum your motherboard supports in its specifications, and whether it has free slots
Buy a matched kit of two identical sticks rather than two different sticks, which run at the slower speed
With the PC off and unplugged, open the case and slot the new RAM in with the clips snapping shut
Power on and confirm the new amount appears in Task Manager > Performance > Memory
Only then enable XMP or EXPO in BIOS, and test stability before leaving it enabled
warnings: Take anti-static precautions before handling RAM. Ground yourself on bare metal first.
Check the RAM type your board supports: DDR4 and DDR5 are not interchangeable. Using the wrong type can damage the slots.
An XMP or EXPO profile that is not stable causes random crashes. If the machine becomes unstable, disable it and run at the default speed.

result_trim_and_maintenance.title: Maintenance that actually helps
result_trim_and_maintenance.diagnosis: With low CPU and low memory use, the remaining software-side fixes are modest but real.
steps: Keep at least 15 to 20 percent of the system drive free, and empty the Recycle Bin
Run the built-in cleanup: search Disk Cleanup, choose the drive, and tick System files to free update leftovers
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup to remove superseded component versions
Run sfc /scannow to verify system files are intact
Restart monthly, which clears temporary memory and driver state
If nothing helps and the drive is an HDD, replacing it with an SSD remains the biggest improvement available
warnings: Avoid third-party 'cleaners'. Many delete files Windows needs and cause slowdowns and update failures.
Do not use defrag on an SSD. TRIM is the correct tool and Windows handles it automatically.
